#2180. CAF African Player of the Year: 10 nominees revealed with Yan Diomande missing, three names spark debate

By Axel Clody | 04 Nov 2026 13:52

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) on Wednesday revealed its list of 10 nominees for the 2026 African Ballon d’Or. It is a prestigious selection, but several choices raise eyebrows.

Three Moroccans, three Senegalese and no sign of Ibrahim Maza or Yan Diomande: the list of 10 candidates for the 2026 African Player of the Year award will fuel plenty of discussion.

Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz, Ismael Saibari, Sadio Mane, Ismaila Sarr, Pape Gueye, Amad Diallo, Yoane Wissa, Antoine Semenyo and Teboho Mokoena have been selected by the Confederation of African Football.

?????? ?? ??? ???? (???) - ???????? #CAFAwards2026 https://t.co/jgE5qPNl4C

The reigning champion, Achraf Hakimi, was crowned in 2025 ahead of Mohamed Salah and Victor Osimhen. The Morocco captain has strong arguments to win a second consecutive award, given his performances with Paris Saint-Germain and Morocco’s run at the World Cup.

He would become the first player to retain the award since Mohamed Salah in 2018 and the first Moroccan to win it twice. Ismael Saibari, who has had a particularly accomplished year, is the other Moroccan candidate, while Brahim Diaz completes Morocco’s strong representation.

The three Senegalese players could turn into a handicap for their country. Sadio Mane remains the most prestigious name, while Ismaila Sarr, brilliant in the Conference League with Crystal Palace, and Pape Gueye have played a part in Senegal’s excellent year. They risk splitting the votes, whereas Hakimi appears the most obvious Moroccan candidate.

The absences of Ibrahim Maza and Yan Diomande are surprising, particularly given some of the names selected. Both are among the candidates for the African Young Player of the Year award.

Maza has established himself at Bayer Leverkusen and with Algeria, while Diomande, who became the most expensive African player in history in the summer transfer window, has stepped up a level at RB Leipzig, Real Madrid and with the Ivory Coast national team.

Their youth does nothing to diminish the value of their performances: age should be neither an advantage nor a ceiling. They finished ninth and fifth respectively in the 2026 Kopa Trophy.

The inclusion of Amad Diallo, despite his qualities and growing importance at Manchester United, appears questionable at the expense of Diomande.

The selections of Yoane Wissa and especially Teboho Mokoena can also be debated. The South African from Mamelodi Sundowns remains a reference on the continent, but his year appears less striking individually than those of several players left out.

Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha could also have laid claim to a place after accompanying his country’s historic run. The CAF selected only outfield players, leaving Cape Verde without a representative despite an exceptional year. Even before the list is reduced to three finalists and the CAF Awards ceremony on 7 December in Lagos, Nigeria, the first selection has already produced some major losers.

#2179. Player Ratings West Ham v Cardiff: Bowen Inspires Incredible Comeback

West Ham produced an extraordinary second-half comeback to rescue a 3-3 draw against Cardiff City, having looked completely shell-shocked as they trudged off at half-time three goals behind. Scott Parker’s first game in charge certainly wasn’t short of incident, with the Hammers seemingly heading for another humiliating defeat.

Joel Moylan’s first-half hat-trick had left West Ham in all sorts of trouble, but three substitutions at the interval helped transform the performance. Goals from Divine Mukasa, Arne Engels and Max Kilman completed a remarkable recovery, with the Hammers almost snatching a winner during a frantic finish.

Jarrod Bowen was the inspiration behind the comeback, although the difference between West Ham’s first and second-half performances was astonishing. Having looked completely devoid of confidence during the opening 45 minutes, the players suddenly discovered some urgency, purpose and attacking quality.

It was certainly a dramatic response to the dreadful performance against West Bromwich Albion, although Parker will have seen plenty of problems that still need addressing.

Made a couple of decent saves and produced one absolutely brilliant long throw that almost released Castellanos. Had little chance with Cardiff’s opening goal, but his decision to charge out of his penalty area, miss the ball completely and collide with Kilman was unnecessarily rash. Another unconvincing performance.

Steady and assured defensively in the first half, but his understanding with Bowen was almost nonexistent. The pair looked like they’d never met each other before. Completely different after the break, when Veltman played with real intensity, provided attacking width and combined excellently with the captain. One of West Ham’s most improved performers.

Some excellent defending, including a particularly impressive one-on-one challenge late in the game. His distribution was also a major positive, regularly pinging accurate balls towards the left flank and producing a lovely through ball to create Kanté’s one-on-one opportunity. One of West Ham’s better players across the 90 minutes.

Made an excellent early tackle but was subsequently booked after Solomon’s dreadful loss of possession exposed the defence. May have got a slight deflection on Cardiff’s opening goal, although there was little he could realistically have done. More than made amends in the 81st minute, showing West Ham’s strikers how to finish with a superb half-volley to equalise.

Actually started very well, winning numerous tackles and recovering possession repeatedly. Unfortunately, his lack of pace was badly exposed by a simple ball over the top, leading to a clumsy and avoidable penalty. He’s a centre-back being asked to play left-back, and it showed. Replaced at half-time.

Made his fair share of tackles and demonstrated some of the value of having a specialist defensive midfielder. Produced a crucial last-ditch challenge to prevent Cardiff from potentially scoring again. However, West Ham still left far too much space in central areas and he was withdrawn at half-time.

Worked hard in a box-to-box role but offered surprisingly little of note for much of the match. Played a decent pass in the build-up to one of Kanté’s attacking runs before making a beautifully timed run beyond Cardiff’s defence to score his first West Ham goal. Took the finish very well, and it was a significant contribution.

West Ham’s most technically accomplished player in the first half, looking comfortable in possession and enjoying the freedom of playing as a number ten. Picked out some lovely passes, including an excellent through ball that Castellanos couldn’t capitalise upon. Took his goal brilliantly, controlling Bowen’s chipped pass with his right foot before finishing delicately with his left. A very encouraging performance.

His performance was a microcosm of West Ham’s entire evening. Anonymous and nervous in the first half, but absolutely commanding in the second. His clever chipped pass created Mukasa’s goal, his long ball started the move for Engels’ strike, and his inswinging delivery provided the equaliser for Kilman.

By the closing stages he was practically running the game, producing a wonderful piece of jiggery-pokery to create a late chance for Mayers before delivering another dangerous inswinging ball that Souček headed on target. Outstanding after the break.

Showed some early purpose with a good run down the left, but his decision-making was dreadful. Repeatedly hesitated when presented with opportunities to shoot or pass, and one particularly poor three-yard ball straight to an opponent led to Kilman’s booking. His final deliveries were ineffective and he struggled to make the most of promising positions. Replaced after 67 minutes, and not before time.

Pretty much anonymous throughout the first half. Repeatedly outpaced when through balls offered him opportunities to run beyond Cardiff’s defence, including one occasion when he was beaten for speed by centre-back Will Fish. Managed a tame shot just before the interval but offered very little. Admittedly, West Ham’s disjointed attacking play hardly helped him. Replaced at half-time.

At least attempted to drop deep and get involved, although his first couple of contributions involved giving the ball away. Headed a decent Veltman cross straight at Trott and failed to connect properly with another Bowen delivery. Improved considerably, producing a good shot from distance before supplying an excellent flick-on for Engels’ goal.

Brought tremendous energy and directness after coming on at half-time. Produced an excellent driving run almost half the length of the pitch, followed by some lovely footwork to twist and turn through Cardiff’s defence. Gave the ball away cheaply on occasion but also forced Trott into a very good save after a wonderful first touch created a one-on-one opportunity. Probably did enough to force his way into Parker’s thoughts for the next game.

Introduced at half-time to replace Morato and provide some much-needed pace at full-back. Won an early tackle and looked more comfortable dealing with the demands of the position. Almost scored a dramatic late winner after making an excellent run to meet Bowen’s chipped delivery at the far post, attempting a left-footed instep volley that went tantalisingly close.

Made more of an attacking impression in his first 30 seconds than Solomon had managed for much of the evening. Immediately dropped his shoulder, cut inside and tried his luck with a shot that went wide. In the 89th minute, produced a stinging effort that Trott could only parry back into his penalty area. Confident, positive and willing to take responsibility.

Introduced in the 88th minute for Veltman. Almost scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner when he met another dangerous inswinging Bowen delivery with a well-directed header, forcing Nathan Trott into an excellent save. Not on the pitch long enough to warrant a numerical rating.

#2176. Cardiff City 3 – 3 West Ham | Final whistle, first impressions

IT took all of eleven minutes for the new manager bubble to burst as the home side opened the scoring and the Cardiff City fans duly launched into ‘you’re getting sacked in the morning’ to welcome West Ham’s Scott Parker into the dugout. To be fair, a cracking strike from Jack Moylan gave Hermansen no chance and as is now customary, the Hammers found themselves playing catch up.

Parker’s West Ham had set up with a back four holding a surprisingly high line, plus Magassa and Engels playing in front of the defenders but the pair were still bisected by the excellent pass that put Moylan through for his goal.

New manager, same misery as three went in before half time – again

Magassa and Kilman went into the book early on, the young Frenchman in particular looking short of match pace. Taty looked isolated – as we’d feared – and the Hammers looked a little short of ideas the half hour mark, hardly venturing into their opponent’s 18 yard box.

The warning signs were there as the awful Morato was beaten a couple of times as the Bluebirds attacked down the left: The stand in left back duly gave away a penalty, again out of position and clambering all over the back of his winger. Two-nil with Hermansen again beaten from a spot kick.

A third came from a corner, headed in at the near post by Moylan – a hat trick in the first half – and Scott Parker might have been questioning his rush to assume control ahead of the international break: Three nil before half time, three goals conceded for a third week in a row and the Hammers booed off by their own fans again.

Piroe warming up with Kanté and Mayers showed three changes at half time as Magassa, Morato and Taty departed.

Mukasa’s lobbed goal after being put through by Bowen put the Irons back in the game, with still half an hour to go and at least giving the travelling supporters something to cheer. Bowen, playing more centrally, started to pull the strings and Piroe went close. Suddenly, from nothing, a Bowen through pass was flicked on by Piroe and Engles, through on goal slotted home like a veteran striker. 3-2: And thousands of Hammers armchair fans were thinking maybe, just maybe.

This was, at least, a fighting response to a half time dressing down and a well deserved barracking from the away fans.

Kanté almost levelled down one end, Hermansen inexplicably flew out and clattered Kilman down the other – almost giving away a fourth in the process- and suddenly, you couldn’t take your eyes off it.

And then – three – three and the roof came off thanks to Max Kilman’s goal from Bowen’s brilliant cross.

Absolutely chaotic scenes in the away end as the incredulous claret and blue army couldn’t believe they’d witnessed a fightback from a team dead and buried at half time.

It could have been four as Trott stretched his fingers to Soucek’s header – agonisingly close as the minutes ticked by. Brilliant second half efforts by Piroe, by Bowen – the man of the match – and excellent impact from Ezra Mayers who might just have found himself a role in Parker’s side.

Nuno’s team in the first half, Parker’s in the  second.

#2175. Getafe vs. Brighton: How to watch, date, time, live stream and TV channel for Conference League fixture

By Matthew Cooper | 04 Nov 2026 13:58

Getafe and Brighton meet in the UEFA Conference League on November 5, with the Spanish side welcoming the Seagulls to the Coliseum for matchday three of the league phase.

The hosts currently sit 20th in the table and are searching for their first win, while the visitors are unbeaten in ninth.

Here, Sports Mole details everything you need to know about how to follow Thursday's match.

The match will kick off at 8pm UK time on Thursday, November 5.

The fixture will take place at the Coliseum, which is the home stadium of Getafe.

The ground has a capacity of 16,500 and Getafe have played there since 1998.

The Conference League match will be shown live on TNT Sports 2, with coverage beginning at 7pm UK time.

UK viewers can stream the match live via HBO Max after TNT Sports moved from Discovery+ to HBO Max earlier this year.

Viewers can access the stream through a standalone TNT Sports subscription or by adding TNT Sports to selected HBO Max entertainment packages.

Highlights of the match will be available on UEFA's website, HBO Max and the TNT Sports Football YouTube channel, while TNT Sports will also post clips on their social media channels.

Getafe have failed to pick up a win in Europe so far this season, drawing 1-1 with Romanian side Universitatea Craiova and losing 5-2 to Swiss team Lugano in their opening fixtures.

Jose Bordalas's men need a positive result against Brighton to boost their hopes of reaching the knockouts and they will take heart from the fact they beat Sevilla 3-1 in La Liga on Sunday.

Brighton, meanwhile, are competing in Europe for the first time since 2024 and they have made a strong start.

The Seagulls have four points from their first two league phase games, having thumped Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris 4-0 before drawing 0-0 with Czech side Jablonec.

#2173. FC Thun 3 Hearts 1: Another bruising Conference League defeat as injury woes worsen

Depleted Hearts’ Conference League bruising was almost totally self-inflicted in a 3-1 defeat by Thun in Switzerland.

Belgian boss Wouter Vrancken was without 10 players through various ailments and the Scottish outfit were dealt another blow in the 22nd minute when defender Jamie McCart put through his own goal in calamitous fashion.

Thun doubled their lead in the 33rd minute through striker Brighton Labeau after more poor defending, this time from skipper Stephen Kingsley – who went off later with an injury – and then Furkan Dursun grabbed a third in the 56th minute before Jambos defender Stuart Findlay reduced the deficit in the 82nd minute with a header.

Hearts were left with one Conference League point out of nine following a 1-1 home draw against Nordsjaelland and a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor.

Thick smoke from a pyro halted the game soon after kick-off but when play resumed after a lengthy delay – there were nine minutes added on at the end of the first half – Hearts winger Josh McPake drew a save from Niklas Steffen with an angled drive that lacked real power.

In the 20th minute McPake’s effort from 25 yards after he had drifted in from the left had the power but was beaten away by the Thun keeper.

There appeared to be nothing untoward on the horizon but then came a Hearts horror show.

There was no real pressure on the Jambos goal when a long ball came into the box but with Lucien Dahler at his shoulder, a simple pass back from McCart somehow evaded Hearts keeper Beau Reus and slipped into the corner of the net.

Thun’s second goal was also gift-wrapped.

The home side broke clear and with pace following a Heart set-piece and when Nils Reichmuth crossed into the box from the right, Kingsley stuck out a leg to clear but the ball went straight to Labeau who swept it into the net from 10 yards out.

Dursun was shown a yellow card for a forearm challenge into the face of Findlay, and it perhaps deserved more punishment.

The interval gave the Tynecastle side time to reset but three minutes after the break, Reus made a diving save from Dursun and an even better one from Reichmuth moments later.

However, the keeper was beaten once again when Dursun got his toe to a Reichmuth cross.

On the hour mark, Nico Maier raced clear of the Hearts defence but although his chip beat Reus, it sped wide of the target.

The night got worse for the rattled visitors as injured Kingsley was replaced by 19-year-old Matthew Gillies, called back from a loan spell at Stenhousemuir.

Malachi Fagan-Walcott’s header from a Jordi Altena free-kick was brilliantly saved by Steffen.

In the 78th minute Jan Bamert had the ball in the net after Steffen tipped a free-kick from substitute Nassim Zoukit on to the bar but was ruled offside, before Findlay headed in a consolation from another Altena free-kick.

#2171. Bristol Rovers vs Cambridge United - prediction, team news, lineups

By Calum Burrowes | 04 Nov 2026 14:45, Last updated: 04 Nov 2026 14:53

The oldest football competition in the world gets underway later this week for clubs across the English Football League, with League Two side Bristol Rovers welcoming third-tier Cambridge United to the Memorial Stadium in the FA Cup first round.

The Gas are currently enduring a seven-game winless run in all competitions and face a U's side managed by Neil Harris, who saw his team thrash Brighton & Hove Albion Under-21s 6-0 in the EFL Trophy earlier this week.

Hoping to reach the second round of the FA Cup for the second consecutive campaign, Bristol Rovers head into Friday night's encounter without a victory since beating Exeter City 1-0 in September.

Steve Evans, who is approaching one year in charge of Bristol Rovers, guided the Gas to a mid-table finish last season after overseeing a nine-game unbeaten run to end the campaign, although they were unable to mount a serious challenge for the playoff places.

Their encouraging form towards the end of last season initially carried into the 2026-27 campaign, with Rovers sitting third in League Two at the end of September after winning five of their opening eight matches.

However, since closing out that month with a narrow victory over the Grecians, Evans's side have endured a miserable October, suffering defeats to Barnet, Shrewsbury Town, Salford City and Fleetwood Town.

That poor run has seen the Gas fall out of the automatic promotion places and slide to 17th in the table, with their 16 points leaving them just four clear of the relegation zone.

Returning to the Memorial Stadium for the first time since their goalless draw with Swindon Town, Rovers will hope some FA Cup magic can help end their three-game winless run at home and rediscover the form that saw them set a club-record 11 consecutive victories on their own turf.

As for Cambridge United, they enter the FA Cup as a League One side for the first time since 2024, having secured an immediate return to the third tier last season by finishing third in League Two with 82 points.

Under former Millwall and Gillingham manager Harris, the U's have adapted well to life back in League One and currently sit just one point outside the playoff places, having collected 21 points from five wins, six draws and three defeats.

Despite their encouraging start, Cambridge are without a league victory in four matches, with draws against Wycombe Wanderers and Sheffield Wednesday coming alongside defeats to Plymouth Argyle and Leyton Orient.

However, following their loss at Brisbane Road to close out October, the U's returned to winning ways in emphatic fashion earlier this week, securing progression from Southern Group G in the EFL Trophy with a 6-0 demolition of Brighton & Hove Albion Under-21s at Cledara Abbey Stadium where Callum Stead scored twice in the convincing victory, while the visitors also had a player sent off.

With no league fixture for more than two weeks, Harris will be keen for his side to build on that momentum by reaching the second round of the FA Cup before turning their attention back to League One, where Cambridge will also be looking to cut down on the number of draws that have hindered their progress, having shared the points more often than any other side in the division.

The sides last met in the FA Cup in December 1971, when the Pirates claimed a 3-0 victory over Cambridge in the second round.

Cambridge United form (all competitions):

Having faced a Fleetwood Town side who produced a shock victory over Arsenal in the EFL Cup just days earlier, Bristol Rovers could name an unchanged starting XI, provided there are no fresh injury concerns.

Captain Alfie Kilgour is expected to remain at the heart of a back three, flanked by Keenan Gough and Irish defender Ciaran Kelly.

Club top scorer Fabrizio Cavegn should lead the line, while Jack Sparkes is likely to retain his place in midfield.

Cambridge, meanwhile, are expected to make several changes to the side that featured in the EFL Trophy during the week, although Harris could still hand opportunities to fringe players against opposition from the division below.

Jake Eastwood has been the U's first-choice goalkeeper this season but could make way for 22-year-old Gabriel Breeze, who kept a clean sheet against Brighton's youth side on Tuesday night.

Ben Knight was absent from the squad for that EFL Trophy victory but could return to the attack, with former Barnet forward Stead expected to lead the line once again.

Young; Gough, Kilgour, Kelly; James, Smallwood, Mola, Sparkes; Forde, Cavegn, Appiah

Cambridge United possible starting lineup:

Breeze; Heffernan, Watts, Perry; Bennett, Hoddle, McLoughlin, Bradshaw; Knight, Stead, Heath

Although neither side enjoyed a particularly impressive October, Cambridge will take confidence from their emphatic EFL Trophy victory earlier this week.

We expect the difference in league positions to prove decisive on Friday night, with the visitors securing a comfortable win to progress to the second round of the FA Cup.

#2170. Report: Liverpool increasingly likely to sanction January exit for player in ‘agonising’ situation

One Liverpool player seems increasingly likely to leave Anfield in January as his situation on Merseyside becomes ‘increasingly agonising’.

Having struggled for starts in two seasons under Arne Slot, Federico Chiesa would no doubt have been hoping that a change of head coach might’ve provided the springboard towards an increase in game-time.

Instead, the 29-year-old’s standing at LFC has diminished even further, having played just two minutes under Andoni Iraola so far despite recovering from a back injury almost a month ago.

According to Dean Jones for Flashscore, a January exit from Liverpool for the forward seems ‘increasingly possible’, and a return to his native Italy ‘could provide an attractive solution’ for both player and club.

Lazio, Inter Milan and Roma have been touted as clubs who ‘could explore the possibility’ of bringing Chiesa back to Serie A after he left Juventus for the Reds in 2024, although any such move would depend on what kind of deal the Merseysiders are prepared to consider.

The report adds that the 29-year-old’s situation ‘is becoming increasingly agonising’ as he continues to struggle for game-time at Anfield.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

That Chiesa didn’t even make the substitutes’ bench against Arsenal on Sunday despite being fit and available is a damning indictment of where he stands in the pecking order.

The additions of Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola over the summer added further competition for places in the forward line, and the form of Lewis Koumas has seen him leap ahead of the Italian in the queue.

Iraola had six forwards either as starters or substitutes at the weekend, and he still has Hugo Ekitike to return from injury, so Chiesa is effectively our eighth-choice attacker.

His status at Liverpool was summed up a few weeks ago by Roy Keane’s throwaway comment of ‘Is he still there?‘ when the 29-year-old’s name was mentioned on the Stick To Football podcast, and the situation hasn’t gotten any better for our number 14 in the meantime.

Barring a substantial injury crisis in the forward line (heaven forbid), it’s hard to see the Italian getting much of a look-in at Anfield any time soon, and it’s looking increasingly likely that he could be allowed to leave for his homeland in January.

It’d be a shame of his time with the Reds petered out to that extent, but Chiesa would depart as a genuine cult hero among Kopites for what he has contributed over the past two-and-a-bit years.

#2169. Cardiff City 3 – 3 West Ham United | The morning after..

An absolutely mental evening still feels like a win the next morning, despite West Ham leaving behind another two Championship points.

On a night when league leaders Middlesborough lost to Wrexham (the same Wrexham who lost 6 – 0 to the Irons just a few weeks ago), West Ham United somehow managed to close the gap by a point after being 3 – 0 down, out and destroyed at half time.

Trying to pick out any performance of merit in that first half is likely to be fruitless, such was the extent of the Hammers’ capitulation.

Whether it was the stinging rebuke of 3000 away fans booing them off at half time, a dressing room dressing-down or inspired substitutions –  who knows – but the Hammers suddenly restarted with purpose, pace and directness.

Time, surely, in the international break which lies ahead for Parker to stamp his character on this West Ham side.  Compared with such a weak, floundering first half from Morato, Solomon and Castellanos, their replacements Piroe, Autsbø (better late than never) and Mayers looked relative world beaters.

Scott Parker, remember, brought Areola to Fulham in 2020 and with Hermansen conceding nine goals in the last three without even laying a glove on any of them, he simply has to go.

Plenty of cause for optimism: The transformation of Maximilian Kilman and Jarrod Bowen from anonymous to game-changers typified the metamorphosis of the whole side – which can only have been due to what went on in the dressing room at half time.

Engels’ excellent goal was his first for West Ham and typified the Irons’ second half performance

Engels and Mukasa both looking like genuine attacking midfielders in the second half, both scoring really well taken goals.

Everything that had been missing from Nuno’s half time responses seemed to unfurl before our very eyes, as a team seemingly on a mission came out in the second half.

After that showing I’m confident of three or four changes on Parker’s team sheet when it is announced on Saturday – whereas you’d feel sure his predecessor would have stuck to his same eleven, with unsurprisingly the same results forthcoming, stubborn to the last.

#2168. Venezia vs Udinese - prediction, team news, lineups

By Jonathan O'Shea | 04 Nov 2026 15:04, Last updated: 04 Nov 2026 15:06

The Serie A weekend will kick off with a battle at the bottom under Friday night lights, as Udinese visit Venezia at Stadio Penzo.

After Kosta Runjaic was sacked earlier this week, both clubs have already changed manager due to a truly dismal set of results.

Promoted back to Italy’s top flight last spring, Venezia have only picked up three points since returning to Serie A, and they are rooted to the foot of the table.

After a slow start, the Lagunari swapped Giovanni Stroppa for survival specialist Davide Nicola, whose new side impressively upset Napoli in his first match.

However, they have since lost their next three games without scoring; last weekend, they were beaten 1-0 by Como, despite the best efforts of busy goalkeeper Filip Stankovic.

As a result, Venezia are only the third team ever to lose at least nine of their first 10 Serie A fixtures, leaving Nicola with issues to fix at both ends.

Not only have the Arancioneroverdi scored just six league goals, they are currently conceding at a rate of two per game - undoubtedly relegation form.

Now, they will host opponents in similarly dire shape; as Udinese are just two points above them, victory would lift Venezia off the bottom rung.

Most date back several years, but Udinese have won five of the sides' last seven league meetings, and they came out on top in a Coppa Italia tie earlier this term.

However, they have only ever posted one top-flight victory at Stadio Penzo, and the Fruilani are currently in freefall.

After a 5-2 crushing by Roma last week, Udinese have lost seven of their last eight matches, and that heavy home defeat proved the final stand for Runjaic.

The German coach had fared well in his first two years at the club, but a tally of five points from 10 Serie A games represents their worst start this century.

Without missing a beat, ex-Venezia boss Paolo Zanetti was appointed until the end of the season, and he must first visit his former club.

Since getting the Lagunari promoted for the first time in 19 years, Zanetti's personal record has been mixed elsewhere, so he will surely have a point to prove on Friday.

Marin Sverko, Bartol Franjic and Andrea Adorante are still ruled out for Venezia, while wing-back Thierry Correia is struggling to recover from a thigh strain.

After Lion Lauerbach started the Lagunari's last two matches, it remains to be seen if John Yeboah reforms his partnership with club-record signing Akor Adams.

Only Roma star Donyell Malen (15) has had more shots on target than Adams (13) in Serie A this term, but the Nigerian striker has only scored twice - both times on home turf.

Meanwhile, Udinese's main man is enduring a much leaner run: since the end of March, Keinan Davis has gone 13 league games without finding the net.

Attacking midfielder Jurgen Ekkelenkamp is the Friulani's top Serie A scorer with three goals, and he should certainly feature in Zanetti's first XI.

Although Oumar Solet has overcome a calf problem, the visitors will be without Alessandro Zanoli, David Alaba and Idrissa Gueye; the matchwinner when these teams recently clashed in the cup, Vakoun Bayo remains a doubt.

Stankovic; Halhal, Moreno, Jesus; Hainaut, Perez, Busio, Sohm, Mazzocchi; Yeboah, Adams

Okoye; Abankwah, Solet, Palma; Vojvoda, Karlstrom, Piotrowski, Kamara; Zaniolo, Ekkelenkamp; Davis

With the worst goal difference and fewest points in Serie A, this pair have been in desperate form for most of the season.

Perhaps a 'new manager bounce' can help Udinese finally stir from their malaise, as Zanetti makes a triumphant return to the Penzo.

#2167. The turning point that inspired Celtic to big European victory against Besiktas

On Guy Fawkes night, Celtic finally provided some European fireworks. Martin O'Neill's side got their Europa League campaign up and running with an enthralling 3-2 win over Besiktas.

Junior Olaitain put the visitors ahead in the 54th minute, scoring from the rebound of his own penalty kick that was initially saved by Sam Johnstone.

Celtic Park was engulfed by an all too familiar feeling before O'Neill introduced Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran in the 60th minute.

Osmand scored the equaliser seconds after coming on, with Duran latching on to the youngster's through ball to round Alex Nubel and put Celtic ahead with 12 minutes remaining.

Orkun Kokcu's pile-driver levelled things up for less than 120 seconds as Duran struck again in the 88th minute to give Celtic a priceless victory.

Here are the key talking points from Parkhead...

Celtic's Callum Osmand scored against Besiktas. (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA)

O’Neill made five changes from Sunday’s defeat at Falkirk, most notably drafting Jordan Lotomba in for his first start at right-back.

The Switzerland international had played just 31 minutes in green-and-white hoops before Besiktas, making his inclusion all the more surprising.

Lotomba was tasked with keeping Besiktas' left side quiet though former Arsenal attacker Leandro Trossard and Ernest Poku kept him well occupied.

The 28-year-old sought to maraud forward when he could, but once tripped up on his own feet when attempting a series of step-overs in the opposition third.

The concession of a second-half penalty compounded Lotomba's tough evening. He was withdrawn in the 60th minute for Colby Donovan.

Elsewhere, Kasper Hogh, James Forrest, and Sebastian Tounekti made up a second string frontline.

Duran, Celtic’s top scorer this season, dropped to the bench along with Haissem Hassan. But it wasn’t a completely rotated XI.

Regulars Kieran Tierney, Cameron Carter-Vickers, Liam Scales, and captain Callum McGregor all began, with Benjamin Nygren and Mika Baur also in from the off.

That said, it was the first time O’Neill hadn’t gone full strength in Europe this season, perhaps indicating his feelings at Celtic’s current plight.

There are dull halves of football, and then there are dull halves of football. Besiktas enjoyed the majority of possession (61 per cent) in the opening 45 minutes without mustering many opportunities.

Celtic's sound structure limited the visitors' attacking play. Carter-Vickers defended ably but O'Neill's side struggled to get forward themselves.

By the break, Celtic had just one shot on goal, two touches in the opposition box, and 73 per cent pass accuracy, compared to around 88 per cent in their first three Europa League defeats.

Yet again, their inability to progress play through the lines was apparent. Celtic resorted to going long on a number of occasions. Hogh failed to make it stick and Tounekti struggled greatly.

Besiktas were quite content to pop the ball around, without taking any major risks. You still felt the Turks had a few more gears to move through.

Celtic shouldn't have needed a second-half wake-up call but just seconds after the interval, Trossard fired just shy of the left post.

Moments later, Johnstone's clearance ricocheted off the Belgian attacker and into Lotomba's right-back area. The Celtic defender slid needlessly in on Poku and referee Sascha Stegemann pointed to the spot without hesitation.

Olaitan stepped up and Johnstone made a heroic save that flew into the smoke-filled Glasgow sky, only for the initial taker to score on the rebound.

Just like Johnstone, Lotomba almost redeemed himself in the following seconds, driving forward from his defensive position before tumbling over the ball when attempting to shoot.

But Besiktas weren't ahead for long. O'Neill looked to his bench for fresh impetus on the hour mark and within just a minute of coming on, Osmand scored.

McGregor latched brilliantly on to a loose midfield pass and cut back for the substitute, who scored with practically his first touch.

Celtic Park had all of a sudden rediscovered its European voice.

For the goal, McGregor looked like his old self, driving forward from the engine room to kickstart a promising attack and Osmand provided the killer touch with his first European goal.

If O'Neill's plan was to wait until the game opened up in the second half and then call on the cavalry, it worked a treat.

Just 16 minutes after Osmand drew Celtic level with a fine strike of his own, he turned provider, playing a slide-rule pass in behind Besiktas' defence for Duran.

The Colombian got there ahead of Nubel and slotted beyond the goal line to turn the game on its head.

Duran didn't have to wait long to make his presence felt again, once more beating Nubel, this time from close range, after brilliantly controlling Tierney's mishit shot. It came seconds after Kokcu's leveller.

A true difference-maker, Duran is now up to 13 goals for the season. His impact could not have been greater here.

Well, who saw that coming? After four matchdays, Celtic are finally up and running in the Europa League. It really was now or never for O'Neill's charges, who have given their chances of progression to the knockout stages fresh hope with an unlikely victory.

Beyond their run of six defeats in ten leading into Thursday night, what made the win even more unexpected was the fact Besiktas are the best side they've played at home in the league phase so far.

Celtic struggled greatly against both Ferencvaros and Celta Vigo on their own turf, flailing whenever faced with adversity. They went down meekly in Lisbon too, losing 4-1 to Benfica last month.

No one should get carried away based on one result. Celtic still need somewhere in the region of six to eight points to finish in the top 24 and three out of their four remaining fixtures are away.

The next comes in Leiria against Portuguese second tier side Torreense after the international break. They could realistically gain three more points there before a trip to face Omonia Nicosia in December. Ties against Marseille and Union St-Gilloise lie ahead in January.

O'Neill will take great satisfaction from a European result that's long evaded his team. Time will define its influence on Celtic's wider Europa League picture.

#2166. West Ham Show Their Worst And Best In Extraordinary Cardiff Draw

West Ham’s extraordinary 3-3 draw against Cardiff City was quite possibly the most bizarre game I’ve watched this season. At half-time, with Scott Parker’s new team trailing by three goals, I genuinely wondered whether we were about to concede six or seven. We hadn’t just been beaten in that opening 45 minutes; we’d completely capitulated.

Yet somehow, the same group of players emerged for the second half and produced a performance almost unrecognisable from what had gone before. West Ham dominated Cardiff, scored three goals and could quite easily have won the game. Jarrod Bowen, who had been largely anonymous before the break, suddenly looked like the best player on the pitch by an absolute mile.

I would love to know what Scott Parker said at half-time, because whatever happened in that dressing room had an extraordinary effect. This was a manager who hadn’t even taken a training session with his new players, yet the transformation was incredible. Whether it was his words, the substitutions or simply the players finding something within themselves, I haven’t seen a turnaround quite like it for a long time.

The frustrating thing was that West Ham actually started reasonably well. There was some intensity, some urgency and a willingness to compete for second balls that had been conspicuously absent during the final weeks of Nuno Espírito Santo’s reign.

Parker’s first team selection included Soungoutou Magassa as a specialist defensive midfielder, while Divine Mukasa was given the freedom to play further forward. Both decisions made sense to me, particularly after watching Mukasa spend so much time trying to compensate for problems elsewhere in midfield under Nuno.

Morato was winning tackles, Mukasa looked comfortable on the ball and West Ham appeared to be playing with a little more purpose. Unfortunately, it didn’t last.

After 11 minutes, Joel Moylan was afforded far too much space outside the penalty area and unleashed an absolute thunderbolt into the top corner. There may have been a slight deflection off Max Kilman, but the bigger concern was the amount of room Cardiff had been allowed in central areas.

Even then, West Ham weren’t completely out of the contest. However, the confidence began draining out of the players, and what followed was a collapse that reminded me of everything we’ve been watching for far too long.

In the 37th minute, a simple long ball over the top exposed Morato’s lack of pace at left-back. He couldn’t recover, conceded a penalty and Moylan duly converted to double Cardiff’s advantage.

Two minutes later, it was 3-0. An inswinging corner was met by Moylan at the near post, with Jarrod Bowen somehow finding himself responsible for challenging him in the air. Moylan completed his hat-trick, and West Ham’s defending was absolutely dreadful.

Three goals conceded in three completely different ways: a long-range shot, a straightforward ball over the top and a corner. It was almost as though Cardiff were being invited to choose how they wanted to score next.

What concerned me most wasn’t simply the defending. It was the complete disappearance of confidence.

West Ham looked shell-shocked. Players who had started the match with some urgency suddenly appeared frightened of making mistakes. There was no cohesion, no understanding and precious little belief.

I genuinely feared the worst. Having watched the dreadful defeat against West Bromwich Albion just days earlier, this felt like another team completely falling apart.

There appears to be some serious footballing PTSD within this group after years of being crap. The moment something goes wrong, the confidence seems to disappear, and one setback quickly becomes two or three.

At half-time, I wasn’t wondering how West Ham could get back into the match. I was wondering how many more Cardiff might score.

Parker made three substitutions at the interval, introducing Ezra Mayers, Mohamadou Kanté and Joël Piroe in place of Morato, Magassa and Taty Castellanos.

They were bold changes, but they were absolutely necessary. West Ham needed more pace, more energy and a completely different approach to the game.

Mukasa scored West Ham’s first goal in a remarkable comeback

Suddenly, West Ham were pressing Cardiff, winning possession and moving the ball forward with purpose. There was an intensity to their play that simply hadn’t existed during the closing stages of the first half.

Joël Veltman began getting forward down the right, combining with Bowen and providing genuine attacking width. Kanté brought tremendous energy to midfield, carrying the ball forward and running directly at Cardiff’s defence.

Even Joël Piroe, despite a couple of poor early touches, was at least dropping deeper and attempting to become involved in the game.

West Ham were playing much more directly, regularly looking for balls behind Cardiff’s defence rather than simply passing possession around without any real threat. It wasn’t always pretty, and at times it was almost route-one football, but it was causing Cardiff enormous problems.

The home side had looked completely comfortable before half-time. Now they were struggling to cope with the speed and aggression of West Ham’s attacking play.

I don’t know precisely what Parker said to the players during the interval, but I’d have loved to have been a fly on the wall.

Of course, the tactical changes made a difference, but this was about more than tactics. The players suddenly looked as though they believed they could compete again.

The comeback began in the 57th minute with a genuinely lovely goal from Divine Mukasa.

Bowen produced a beautifully weighted chipped pass over the Cardiff defence, and Mukasa timed his run perfectly. His control with his right foot was exquisite before he delicately lifted the ball over Nathan Trott with his left.

It was a wonderful piece of football and exactly the sort of attacking quality we’ve been crying out for.

More importantly, it gave West Ham something to believe in.

The Hammers continued pushing forward, with Bowen becoming increasingly influential and Veltman offering support down the right. Cardiff were beginning to look uncomfortable, particularly when West Ham played early balls into the space behind their defensive line.

In the 65th minute, another direct ball from Bowen was cleverly flicked on by Piroe. Arne Engels timed his run beautifully and finished past Trott to make it 3-2.

From looking completely dead and buried, West Ham were suddenly within one goal of an equaliser.

Kanté produced an excellent opportunity after Mavropanos picked him out with a lovely pass. His first touch was superb, but Trott made a brilliant save to deny him.

Cardiff were retreating deeper and deeper, desperately trying to protect their lead. West Ham, meanwhile, were playing with a confidence and attacking intent that had been completely absent just half an hour earlier.

It was extraordinary to watch the transformation in our captain. In the first half, he had looked just as nervous and uncertain as everyone else. After the break, almost everything good West Ham produced seemed to involve him.

He was drifting into central areas, creating opportunities, playing clever passes and generally dictating proceedings.

In the 81st minute, West Ham finally got the equaliser their second-half performance deserved.

A corner initially appeared to have come to nothing, but Bowen kept the attack alive and swung another dangerous ball into the penalty area. Max Kilman was still forward and produced a superb half-volley to beat Trott.

I could scarcely believe what I was watching.

The remarkable thing was that West Ham weren’t satisfied with rescuing a point. They continued attacking and looked the more likely side to score a winner.

Edvin Austbø, who had replaced Manor Solomon, brought an immediate willingness to run at defenders. In the 89th minute, he unleashed a powerful shot that Trott could only parry back into his penalty area.

There was a real whiff of panic about Cardiff by this stage. Having been three goals ahead at half-time, they now looked desperate for the final whistle.

A minute later, Bowen produced another wonderful piece of jiggery-pokery before chipping the ball towards the far post. Ezra Mayers made an excellent run into the penalty area and attempted a left-footed volley that went tantalisingly close.

Even in stoppage time, West Ham were still creating opportunities.

In the 92nd minute, Bowen delivered yet another dangerous inswinging ball, this time finding Tomáš Souček. The midfielder directed his header on target, only for Trott to produce an excellent save.

It would have been an extraordinary winner, but even without a fourth goal, West Ham had completed a comeback that looked utterly impossible at half-time.

I suspect Cardiff were extremely grateful there weren’t another ten minutes left to play.

By Matt Law | 04 Nov 2026 15:53, Last updated: 04 Nov 2026 15:58

Sevilla will be aiming to return to winning ways in Spain's top flight when they welcome Alaves to Estadio Ramon on Friday evening.

The home team are currently sixth in the La Liga table, picking up 17 points from 11 matches, while Alaves are 11th in the division, claiming 12 points from 11 games.

Sevilla boast a record of five wins, two draws and four defeats from their 11 league matches this season, with 17 points leaving them in a European spot in the division, sitting sixth.

It has been a difficult period of the season for Luis Garcia Plaza's side, who have only been victorious in one of their last five matches in Spain's top flight.

Sevilla will enter this game off the back of a 3-1 defeat to Getafe, with their last success coming in their last home league fixture - a 2-0 victory over Osasuna.

Los Nervionenses finished 13th in Spain's top flight last season, but they have the look of a team capable of challenging for a European finish this term.

Sevilla have won 21 of their previous 45 matches against Alaves, suffering 12 defeats in the process, but it was 1-1 when the pair last locked horns in February 2026.

Alaves have only actually lost one of their last seven matches against Sevilla, recording four wins in the process, so the visitors should enter this game in a confident mood.

The Blue and Whites suffered a 6-1 defeat to Barcelona last time out, and a tough run of form has seen them pick up just two points from their last seven matches.

Alaves have not been victorious in the league since the start of September, when they recorded a 5-2 win over Osasuna, and their recent struggles have seen them drop down the table, currently sitting 11th with 12 points from 11 matches.

Quique Sanchez Flores' side are just two points off the relegation zone but also only three points behind seventh-placed Athletic Bilbao, so a lot could change with a victory in this match.

Alaves are enjoying a strong period in their history given that nine of their last 10 seasons have been played in the top flight of Spanish football.

Sevilla will be without the services of Manu Bueno, with the midfielder sent off in the team's 3-1 defeat to Getafe last time out.

Bueno had actually been substituted into the match for Isaac Romero, who suffered an injury, and the striker is regarded as a major doubt for this contest.

There will also be absences for Marcao and Miguel Sierra, with the pair unavailable due to muscular and shoulder injuries respectively.

As for Alaves, Facundo Garces and Mikel Rodriguez are both out of the match through injury, but the visitors did not suffer any fresh issues against Barcelona.

Head coach Sanchez Flores is expected to resist the temptation to shuffle his pack despite the disappointing nature of the result against the La Liga champions.

Toni Martinez is expected to be introduced back into the side, while there will be a spot in the final third of the field for Lucas Boye, who has netted five league goals this term.

#2164. Scott Parker Moves Quickly To Fix West Ham Coaching Concern

West Ham United have confirmed that Jonathan Hill has joined Scott Parker’s backroom team as assistant coach, bringing additional experience to the Hammers’ new management setup. Hill has previously worked alongside Parker at several clubs and arrives with a strong background in football analysis.

The appointment was announced on West Ham’s official website, with Hill joining Mark Noble, Steve Potts, Gerard Prenderville and Billy Lepine on the coaching staff.

It was only after West Ham’s remarkable 3-3 draw against Cardiff City in Parker’s first match as Hammers boss that I discovered he’d added another member to his backroom team. And I have to say, I’m absolutely delighted.

I think having Mark Noble in the dugout is incredible. His passion for West Ham, understanding of the club and ability to connect with players should bring something invaluable to the dressing room.

But the one concern I had about Noble’s appointment was his lack of extensive first-team coaching experience.

That isn’t a criticism of Noble, far from it. I just felt Parker needed somebody alongside him with a strong background in coaching and tactical analysis.

By bringing in Jonathan Hill, he has immediately addressed what I considered a glaring gap in the backroom team.

Hill’s previous working relationship with Parker should also be an advantage. There is already an understanding between the two, rather than the new head coach having to build that relationship from scratch.

And nobody who witnessed the first half against Cardiff can be in any doubt that this West Ham squad will benefit from all the additional coaching and tactical expertise it can get.

The players clearly have ability, as the comeback demonstrated, but there is still an enormous amount of work to do.

For me, this is an encouraging appointment. Parker has retained the West Ham connections and passion that Noble and Potts provide, while adding another experienced football man to help with the coaching.

It’s early days, of course, but I’m pleased to see the new manager strengthening his staff so quickly.

#2163. ‘Matter of fact’ – Virgil van Dijk issues Liverpool reality check after defeat to Arsenal

Virgil van Dijk has advised Liverpool to forget about what their Premier League rivals are doing and concentrate on themselves, following the defeat to Arsenal at the weekend.

The Reds now trail the champions and leaders by nine points after the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday, and Daily Mail writer Ian Ladyman said that the result shows that Andoni Iraola’s side are ‘not ready‘ to properly contend for the top-flight title this season.

It was a second home defeat in the space of a month for LFC, who were also beaten on their own patch by second-placed Manchester City, and the veteran Dutch defender acknowledged that his team are in a transitional phase after changing head coach over the summer.

Speaking to reporters after the defeat to Arsenal, Van Dijk proclaimed (via Liverpool Echo): “We have to just focus on ourselves.

“I don’t think it is good to think about the other two [Arsenal and Man City] and even [third-placed] Brighton. We have to focus on ourselves and we are in a process.

“We have been together now for four months but we play at Liverpool and we want results every three days, especially at home.

“The main thing is we keep working very hard and that we see improvement, but the matter of fact is we are in a transition. [Arsenal] was a great opportunity to get a good result, but unfortunately it didn’t happen, so we have to take it.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Nobody realistically expected Liverpool to challenge for the title at the start of the season, so it wouldn’t be a failure if the Reds aren’t in contention for the trophy by the time April rolls around.

The objective for this campaign was to finish closer to the summit and show discernible improvement on a wretched 2025/26, and recent performances suggest that Iraola is capable of delivering in that regard.

His team are currently on course to end the season with 63 points (just three more than last term), but if they improve on a home record of just one win from five league games so far, they should be able to nudge that projected total into the 70s.

Liverpool competed admirably with Arsenal and Man City (up until the harsh red card for Ryan Gravenberch) but weren’t as clinical as the top two in those games. With more ruthlessness in attack, the Reds seem capable of at least closing that gap.

Van Dijk is correct – the goal for this season isn’t to compete for the title, but to qualify for the Champions League with relative comfort and lay the foundations for further improvement in 2027/28.

There’s still plenty of room for improvement, but at least there are signs of this campaign being much more convincing than 2025/26 had been.

It is the first time that Leicester have competed in this round since 2008, and Oxford City have been given the chance to claim a huge scalp in the tournament.

Oxford City have managed to progress to the second round of the FA Cup on three previous occasions - 1969-70, 2017-18 and 2020-21, so the club have previous when it comes to advancing past this stage of the famous cup competition.

The Hoops will enter this match off the back of a disappointing result, though, going down 3-1 at home to South Shields in the National League North on Saturday.

Ross Jenkins' side are currently second in the National League North, picking up 27 points from their opening 14 matches of the campaign, two points behind South Shields following the clash between the top two.

Oxford City have had to win three matches to reach this stage of the FA Cup, overcoming Dorchester, Enfield Town and Torquay to be present in the first round.

Leicester, meanwhile, will enter this match off the back of a 2-2 draw with Stevenage, with the result leaving them in 10th spot in the League One table.

The Foxes have won three of their last five league games, but there is no getting away from the fact that it has been a disappointing start to the season as a whole.

Leicester famously won this competition back in 2021, recording a 1-0 victory over Chelsea courtesy of a second-half effort from Youri Tielemans.

Russell Martin is still under pressure at Leicester but remains at the helm, with the 40-year-old bidding to help the Foxes secure a return to the Championship.

#2161. “Forceful and Aggressive” Parker’s Passion Already Making A Mark At West Ham

West Ham manager Scott Parker’s comments following last night’s incredible comeback against Cardiff City were an absolute joy to listen to. Having watched the Hammers recover from three goals down to draw 3-3, I was already feeling considerably more optimistic about our prospects. But listening to Parker afterwards was almost as encouraging as the second-half performance itself.

In the modern game, much is made of tactics, and rightly so. But one thing I believe gets underplayed is not only man-management, but a head coach’s personality. And quite frankly, Parker has bundles of it.

I have to say, it’s a refreshing change from what we’ve seen in recent seasons. Nuno Espírito Santo was a softly spoken man, not prone to using a few words when considerably more would do, and the less said about Graham Potter as a leader and orator, the better at this point. But my word, it’s thrilling to hear Parker speak.

Speaking in his post-match interview with West Ham’s official website, Parker described the transformation in his team after the break:

“It was a forceful team, an aggressive team, a front-footed team, which was obviously a big improvement.”

That’s exactly what I want to hear from a West Ham manager, and more importantly, it’s exactly what I want to see from a West Ham team.

As Martins morning round-up demonstrated, the difference between the two halves was extraordinary.

We went from a team seemingly incapable of stringing together a meaningful attack to one that looked determined to take the game to the opposition.

And Parker clearly recognised the difference.

He was particularly critical of the backwards passing and the lack of purpose in possession during the opening 45 minutes.

Then came another observation that I found particularly encouraging:

“There’s no point in just building, building, building.”

Again, music to my ears and we saw that with the first two goals from Mukasa and Engels.

For far too long, we’ve watched West Ham move the ball around without appearing particularly interested in doing anything with it.

Parker wants players taking risks, making forward runs, delivering crosses and getting bodies into the penalty area.

That doesn’t guarantee success, of course, but it’s a pretty good place to start.

What really impressed me, though, wasn’t simply Parker’s analysis of the football.

It cannot be overstated quite how much good it does the fanbase to see a manager walking over to applaud the travelling supporters, becoming one with them, and then speaking so passionately about what he wants to achieve.

There were 3,200 West Ham fans at Cardiff, and after the dreadful opening 45 minutes, they deserved something to cheer.

And I’ll tell you this much: if Parker communicates with supporters like this, one can only imagine how effective he might be when speaking to his players.

Of course, being a good speaker doesn’t automatically make somebody a good manager.

But I’ve always believed that one of the most immediate improvements West Ham needed was motivation.

We have talented players. I’ve said that repeatedly. What we’ve lacked is somebody capable of getting them playing with urgency, belief and a bit of fire in their bellies.

Parker certainly sounds like somebody who understands that.

I was also absolutely delighted to hear him say how eager he was to get the players together and start asking questions.

He admitted that he couldn’t fully understand how the performance had changed so dramatically between the two halves.

And rather than simply celebrating the comeback, he was already thinking about what needed to improve before Saturday’s trip to Blackburn Rovers.

It’s also worth remembering that Parker had only met the players at the airport that morning, having been confirmed as West Ham’s new head coach just hours before kick-off.

He has barely had an opportunity to work with them.

Judging his tactics, selections and long-term suitability can come later. There will be plenty of time for that.

But I’ve always thought there was one obvious and immediate improvement that could be made to this West Ham team, and that was getting the players motivated.

After listening to Parker, I have considerably fewer worries on that score.

I genuinely cannot wait for the next game.

#2160. Mark Noble’s Return To West Ham Dugout Comes With A Catch

The sight of Mark Noble sitting alongside Scott Parker in last night’s game has prompted plenty of debate among West Ham supporters.

For many, the question is simple. If Noble does not hold the UEFA coaching qualifications, how can he be part of the first-team setup and occupy a place on the bench?

The issue has become a hot topic among supporters, particularly as UEFA regulations require coaches working at various levels of the professional game to hold the appropriate licences or be actively working towards them. UEFA’s coaching pathway runs from C Licence through to Pro Licence, with increasing levels of qualification required for senior positions.

However, the reality is that not everyone seated in a technical area is necessarily registered as a coach.

Modern football clubs employ a wide variety of football staff whose responsibilities can overlap with the first team without them formally holding coaching positions. Player liaison officers, football advisers, technical assistants, performance specialists and football operations staff can all be involved on matchdays without being registered as coaches.

That distinction could prove crucial in understanding Noble’s position.

He brings invaluable experience and knowledge to the team. Few individuals understand the pressures and expectations of representing West Ham better than the club’s former captain. His influence around a dressing room, particularly during periods of transition, could be viewed as every bit as important as the contribution of a traditional coach.

Nevertheless, the situation raises an understandable question among fans. Yet as his role continues to evolve, supporters will remain curious about the precise nature of his responsibilities and whether formal coaching qualifications may eventually become part of his longer-term pathway in football.

#2159. Wouter Vrancken demands unity as Hearts seek to bounce back from Thun defeat

Wouter Vrancken insists Hearts will have to stick together following their self-inflicted 3-1 Conference League defeat by Thun in Switzerland.

The Scottish outfit, without 10 players through various injuries, fell behind in the 22nd minute when defender Jamie McCart knocked the ball into his own net.

Thun doubled their lead in the 33rd minute through striker Brighton Labeau after a poor attempted clearance from captain Stephen Kingsley – who went off later with an injury – and then Furkan Dursun grabbed a third in the 56th minute.

Jambos defender Stuart Findlay then gave some unrealised hope of a comeback in the 82nd minute when he headed in from close range.

After three Conference League fixtures Hearts have one point out of nine and have won just two of their last 10 fixtures in all competitions.

Vrancken told TNT Sports: “Like I said already to the guys, we have to stick together now.

“We know which situation we’re in with all the circumstances.

“And there’s only one thing that you have to do now and that is stick together and keep working hard.

“In general, it was not good enough in quality and can you blame them?

“Yeah, on one hand you can because you want to always expect the best and want the best.

“On the other hand, I’m still proud of what they did already in the run-up games.”

Kingsley was replaced in the second half by 19-year-old Matthew Gillies, called back from a loan spell at Stenhousemuir amid the club’s injury crisis, and Vrancken admitted there was an element of risk playing him on the artificial surface which the Jambos boss had criticised.

He said: “We talked it through before the game of course, a few days before the game.

“And yeah, it’s always a risk, especially when it’s another surface, and especially when it’s bad like that, but he was confident in playing and that’s where we are.”

Hearts’ next Conference League game is against Ligue 1 side in Monaco at Tynecastle on November 26 but Vrancken is more concerned about the home William Hill Premiership game against Falkirk on Sunday.

He said: “Monaco’s a really strong side, maybe the strongest side we will face in Europe.

“So we will see when we get there, because I think there are a lot of important games before that, especially on Sunday.”

The hosts have lost five consecutive league matches and are hovering just above the relegation zone with eight points from their opening 10 fixtures, while their visitors occupy fifth place with 17 points and arrive unbeaten in their last three league outings, with a new manager at the helm.

The lack of attacking output is becoming a significant concern for Ak, whose team have struggled to turn possession into meaningful opportunities and have repeatedly found themselves chasing matches after falling behind.

Gaziantep have also struggled to establish Gaziantep Stadyumu as a source of points, failing to win any game as hosts yet, drawing two and losing three times in five home matches.

Gaziantep have several availability concerns ahead of Friday's encounter, with Myenty Abena facing suspension following a yellow-card accumulation, while Ulrich Meleke, Ogun Ozcicek, Arda Kizildag and Sontje Hansen are among those carrying injuries.

Serdar Dursun is also expected to miss out, while Nazim Sangare and Fuat Bavuk remain unavailable.

Kasimpasa have fewer confirmed concerns, although Kamil Ahmet Corekci is expected to remain sidelined with an Achilles tendon injury.

Godfried Frimpong and Kevin Mouanga are also carrying fitness problems, leaving the visitors potentially short of defensive options, while no further suspensions have been reported.

Adrian Benedyczak has scored six goals in the league this season, and he will be the man to watch for the Apaches in this encounter.

#2157. ‘It affected my family’ – VAR official reveals full impact of huge decision which cost Liverpool

The official who was on VAR duty for the wrongly disallowed Luis Diaz goal in Liverpool’s 2-1 defeat to Tottenham in 2023 has spoken about the impact that the controversy had on his family.

The Colombian thought he had put the Reds 1-0 up in the 35th minute of the game in north London, but he was incorrectly flagged for offside, and a subsequent review from Stockley Park saw that erroneous decision upheld.

When the audio from the VAR conversation was publicly released a few days later, it was revealed that Darren England – the official on duty – had given the message of ‘check complete’ to the on-field referee in the mistaken belief that the goal was allowed to stand.

The 40-year-old has given an interview to BBC Sport in which he reflected on the regret from that hugely controversial decision, and how the fallout seeped into his family life.

England recalled: “Once I realised I’d made the error, it’s a really difficult place to try to forget that and move on. I can’t just physically stand up and walk out and leave it alone. A lot of resilience was needed – a lot of experience as well.”

He added: “The aftermath obviously was really difficult to deal with. It was challenging because it’s the goldfish bowl of the Premier League, but when mistakes happen, then you’re in the public eye and criticism’s inevitably going to come your way.

“That was difficult because it affected my family as well. We had people outside my girls’ school, journalists and things like that. That then affects you not as a referee, but as a human being.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The catalogue of errors which led to Diaz’s legitimate goal being disallowed was farcical, with all of the officials on duty collectively culpable for the shambolic process which unfolded.

England did acknowledge in the VAR audio that he thought the on-field decision was onside and immediately held his hands up to the error, but that came as no comfort to anyone associated with Liverpool after such a costly and preventable outcome.

🚨 OFFICIAL: PGMOL have released VAR audio from Spurs v Liverpool 🔊 pic.twitter.com/zNLDyHkBbe

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) October 3, 2023

Criticism of the officials botching the process was inevitable and justified, but obviously the media intrusion into the referee’s family life crossed an unacceptable line, and we can empathise with how difficult the fallout must’ve been for the now 40-year-old.

Unfortunately, more than three years on from that chaotic blunder, refereeing standards in the Premier League haven’t improved to any great extent, as we saw at the weekend with the inexplicable decision not to award a penalty for a clear pull by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak’s shirt.

Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb needs to do much more to ensure that a satisfactory standard of officiating is reached, but no person deserves to have an error in the course of the work turn into an unwarranted invasion on their family life.

#2155. West Ham Owners’ ‘Marriage Of Convenience’ Could End With Staveley Takeover

West Ham’s ownership saga has taken another interesting turn following comments from former football executive Christian Purslow, who believes Daniel Křetínský and David Sullivan could eventually sell the club to Amanda Staveley once the Hammers return to the Premier League.

Speaking to football journalist Henry Winter on The Football Boardroom podcast, Purslow described the relationship between West Ham’s two principal shareholders as a “marriage of convenience” and questioned why the previously announced agreement to purchase Vanessa Gold’s shares has still not been formally completed.

Regular readers of Claret & Hugh, and indeed viewers of Hammers Chat, will not be particularly surprised by any of this. I’ve been describing Sullivan and Křetínský as business partners for some time, and the possibility of Staveley eventually returning to the negotiating table is something we’ve discussed at length.

Purslow’s comments came during a fascinating discussion with Henry Winter about West Ham’s ownership situation, prompted by the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo and the appointment of Scott Parker.

The former Liverpool and Aston Villa chief executive suggested that Sullivan and Křetínský may have very little in common, but they share one overriding ambition: getting West Ham back into the Premier League as quickly as possible.

That, according to Purslow, is enough to keep their working relationship together, even if their longer-term ambitions for the football club are different.

And frankly, I think he’s absolutely right.

Ever since the agreement was reached for Křetínský to purchase the bulk of Vanessa Gold’s shares, with Sullivan increasing his own holding from approximately 38.8% to 40%, I’ve referred to the pair as business partners. Indeed, Claret & Hugh reported last month that a club insider had specifically described their relationship as a “joint partnership”.

I appreciate that this might be uncomfortable for some West Ham supporters to hear, particularly those who hoped Sullivan’s departure from his executive position would signal the beginning of the end of his involvement.

But let’s be fair, a man who wants less financial involvement in a football club doesn’t ordinarily increase his shareholding. Whatever anybody thinks of Sullivan, the proposed arrangement would leave him owning approximately 40% of West Ham, and that’s hardly the behaviour of somebody desperate to walk away immediately.

Staveley has been locked out of West Ham for now

What I found particularly interesting was Purslow questioning something we’ve also discussed repeatedly on this website. Why has the agreement to increase Křetínský’s shareholding to 46% still not been formally completed?

The arrangement was announced back in September, with the existing shareholders exercising their rights to purchase Vanessa Gold’s stake and subsequently agreeing to redistribute shares. As our original investigation into the transaction explained, the process was designed to leave Křetínský as West Ham’s largest shareholder, Sullivan on approximately 40% and Tripp Smith on around 11%.

Yet here we are in November, and the anticipated confirmation of the completed transaction has still not arrived. Purslow admitted he found that puzzling and wondered whether the agreement might have encountered difficulties, although he was careful to acknowledge that he did not know whether that was the case.

I completely agree with him that the delay is odd, although I wouldn’t go so far as to suggest the agreement has collapsed. In fact, when Claret & Hugh last enquired, we were assured that there were no problems with the transaction and that completion was expected soon.

Nevertheless, there is another important point here. Křetínský indicated that he would engage with supporters once his increased shareholding had been finalised, and we’re still waiting for that conversation.

Given the importance of the proposed ownership changes, I don’t think it’s unreasonable for supporters to expect some clarity about when the transaction will be completed and what the future structure of the club will look like.

Kretinsky successfully blocked Vanessa Gold’s attempts to sell her shareholding to Staveley but has yet to purchase her shares according to Purslow

Perhaps the most fascinating part of Purslow’s analysis concerned Amanda Staveley, who previously attempted to purchase the Gold family’s stake before the existing shareholders moved to prevent her from acquiring it.

Purslow suggested that once West Ham have secured promotion to the Premier League, both Sullivan and Křetínský could decide that the time is right to sell the entire football club. He also identified Staveley as a possible buyer, pointing to her previous interest, the work she has already undertaken examining the club and her ambitions for the London Stadium.

His assessment was particularly interesting:

“I have a feeling Amanda Staveley might well reappear because she would be the natural buyer for the whole club.”

Now, this is obviously Purslow’s prediction rather than confirmation of any agreement between the shareholders and Staveley. But I have to say, it’s a scenario I’ve considered entirely plausible for some time.

I’ve never fully believed that Staveley had gone away completely. For somebody who appeared so determined to purchase a football club, there has been remarkably little public indication of her pursuing another opportunity since her attempt to buy into West Ham was blocked.

Of course, that doesn’t mean she hasn’t been exploring other possibilities privately. But we already know she has shown a serious interest in West Ham, and Claret & Hugh previously revealed that discussions had taken place over the possibility of her acquiring Sullivan’s shares if the Gold family route proved unsuccessful.

Purslow also raised the question of valuations. He suggested Staveley’s previous proposal valued West Ham at around £600million, while Sullivan has historically placed a considerably higher value on the club. Promotion would clearly change the financial picture, making a potential sale more attractive than it would be while West Ham remain in the Championship.

The suggestion that Sullivan and Křetínský are effectively working together until West Ham secure promotion makes a certain amount of sense to me. Both have an enormous financial interest in the club returning to the Premier League, and that shared objective could be enough to maintain their partnership regardless of any differences between them.

It also puts the appointment of Scott Parker into an interesting context. Having backed Nuno to lead the promotion campaign during the summer, the shareholders have now agreed to change direction and appoint a manager with three Championship promotions on his CV.

Purslow clearly believes promotion could become the catalyst for something much bigger than another managerial change. His suggestion is that the two principal shareholders might eventually decide to cash in, potentially creating the opportunity for Staveley to return with a proposal to purchase the whole club rather than simply a minority stake.

Whether that happens remains to be seen, and there is certainly no evidence of an agreed sale. But I find it difficult to dismiss the possibility, particularly given everything we’ve already been told about the relationship between Sullivan and Křetínský and Staveley’s previous determination to get involved.

For me, the most revealing aspect of Purslow’s comments is that he has independently arrived at a number of the same questions we’ve been asking for months. Why is the share transaction taking so long? What exactly is the relationship between Sullivan and Křetínský? And has Amanda Staveley really disappeared from the picture?

I suspect we haven’t heard the last of any of those three questions.
